current_episode.title: The intersection of behavioural science, the water sector, and utilities more broadly

guest.bio_context: Arminak Antonian comes from an academic background, having served as an economics professor at Cardiff Business School and previously as a professor of economics in China. He has conducted extensive research and interventions with the Armenian government and the UN in countries including Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Uzbekistan, and Croatia, working on behavioral challenges ranging from cancer screening uptake and health checkups to tax compliance and plastic consumption reduction.

pending_qa.q: What role do smart meters and data analytics play in designing targeted customer interventions?
pending_qa.r: Smart meters and technological advancements allow utilities to understand customer behavior better and tailor interventions accordingly. If a customer has a leak, utilities can send targeted notifications enabling them to resolve the issue. Data allows companies to design tailored interventions for individual customers and create a more customer-centric experience.

pending_qa.q: What are the three categories of demand-side interventions that behavioral science can address in the water sector?
pending_qa.r: Interventions using technology such as smart meters and water-efficient appliances; interventions using audits whether online or offline to identify water waste and check for leaks; and awareness raising campaigns. Behavioral science can enhance adoption of these interventions by understanding customer perspectives and addressing barriers.

pending_qa.q: What does a large-scale behavioral experiment on water audit adoption reveal about customer motivations?
pending_qa.r: Thames Water tested 400,000 smart-metered households with different email approaches including environmental messaging, financial savings messaging, and future generations messaging. Money was the most convincing motivation, followed by environmental concerns. The company subsequently merged these two motives into combined messaging and is now testing whether tailored segment-specific communication performs better than one-size-fits-all bulk emails.

pending_qa.q: Why is social media an unreliable source for understanding overall customer sentiment in utilities?
pending_qa.r: Social media typically shows only the most satisfied and most dissatisfied customers, while the bulk middle of reasonably satisfied customers remain inactive and unexpressed. This creates a misleading picture. Instead, utilities should use brand tracking surveys conducted twice yearly and segment-based experiments to understand true customer attitudes on issues like pollution and water consumption.
